claims.text: 316L is an austenitic stainless steel containing standard baseline levels of Cr and Mo.
Increasing Cr and Mo above their baseline levels enhances the corrosion resistance of austenitic stainless steels.
Increasing Cr and Mo promotes rapid formation of a continuous passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer promoted by increased Cr and Mo is self-healing.
The passive oxide layer promoted by increased Cr and Mo is chemically uniform.
The relevant structural mediator is a Cr- and Mo-enriched passive film whose continuity, adherence, and compactness govern corrosion resistance.
Enhanced Cr and Mo levels accelerate oxidation kinetics.
Enhanced Cr and Mo levels stabilize formation of a self-healing oxide film.
The passive film impedes corrosive ions and thereby reduces metal dissolution in harsh environments.
Corrosion resistance is mediated by the passive film's uniformity and chemical composition.
Cr- and Mo-enriched variants will form a more robust, uniform, and adherent oxide film than baseline 316L.
Cr- and Mo-enriched variants will exhibit significantly lower corrosion current densities than baseline 316L.
XPS and TEM will reveal a uniform passivating layer enriched in Cr and Mo on the modified alloys.
Baseline 316L exhibits typical passive-film formation and corrosion rates.
The proposed mechanism should apply to austenitic stainless steels in high-temperature, high-pressure reactor coolant and acidic chemical-processing environments.
The proposed findings may not extend to other steel classes or substantially different environments.
Increasing Cr and Mo may affect tensile strength and weldability.
